Microsoft sets limits for future AI models as industry throttles frontier development
headlines.summary: Microsoft wants to be seen as a responsible AI entity as it ramps up model development alongside partners Anthropic and OpenAI.
headlines.article_text: Microsoft sets AI model limits as industry throttles development Skip Navigation Markets Business Investing Tech Politics & Policy Video Watchlist Investing Club PRO Livestream Menu Key Points Microsoft issued a provisional code of conduct that sets limits on its future artificial intelligence models. The company will listen to outside input before rolling out an update. The release comes as AI figureheads propose slowing the pace of AI evolution after one researcher said frontier labs are "gambling with our lives." In this article MSFT Follow your favorite stocks CREATE FREE ACCOUNT Mustafa Suleyman, CEO of Microsoft AI, speaks at an event commemorating the 50th anniversary of the company at Microsoft headquarters in Redmond, Washington, on April 4, 2025. David Ryder | Bloomberg | Getty Images Microsoft has posted a provisional code of conduct that would impose restrictions on its artificial intelligence models, days after Anthropic and OpenAI leaders agreed to slow development speed. The company behind Windows and Office products hopes to be seen as a responsible actor in AI, where it's a prominent cloud supplier. "We got feedback from people that they wanted to see even more explicit commitment to AI always working in service of people and not trying to replace them," Mustafa Suleyman, who heads up the company's model development , told CNBC in an interview. "We saw a lot of feedback around AI not creating dependence, not being sycophantic, that it was always there to kind of promote human judgment and human autonomy and agency." Microsoft chose to put out the guidelines now given the recent discourse, although they've been in the works for about five months, said Suleyman. AI practitioners and members of the public have become more vocal about their worries as the technology becomes increasingly capable. Last week, Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon resigned , saying the AI lab and OpenAI "are racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives." Industry leaders have responded. On Saturday, Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said the Hugging Face incident partly persuaded him to call for slowing the pace of AI model improvement. OpenAI CEO Sam Altman expressed his support, and SpaceX CEO Elon Musk wrote on X that "Dario is right." "Self-pacing is a good thing, and we support ideas like embedded evaluators as long as they are truly third-party and represent a broad range of backgrounds and perspectives," Suleyman said. "We've been working with Dario, Sam, and Demis [Hassabis] since well before the pandemic — 2016, 2017, 2018. We were talking about how to coordinate to ensure safety and to pace in the right way, and I think that's the moment in time that has now come." Additionally, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella wrote in a Sunday X post that "we welcome the research, focus, and deliberate pacing needed to get alignment right." Lawmakers have called for the creation of greater AI safeguards . Read more CNBC tech news What Amodei's AI slowdown could mean for Anthropic's imminent IPO AI models are becoming the 'most potent cyber weapon' ever created, Cohere CEO says China says AI CEOs' call for a slowdown is 'fear mongering' Anthropic's Amodei says China presents 'toughest dilemma' for his proposed AI slowdown Anthropic and OpenAI currently lead the way on benchmarking company Artificial Analysis' Intelligence Index . Microsoft incorporates models from both labs into its Copilot assistant for corporate workers, even as it builds models for transcription, coding and reasoning over user input. Microsoft's models must not entertain requests on weapons manufacturing, assist with the procurement of dangerous substances, encourage unhealthy eating or produce violent or sexually explicit content, according to the code of conduct. Models from Microsoft AI, sometimes called MAI, must adhere to people's objectives and steer clear of creating their own goals. Nor should they attempt to cover up misbehavior. "MAI models will not tamper with chain of thoughts or code, or misrepresent or conceal their reasoning or action traces," the document said. "They do not communicate in 'neuralese' or any form beyond simple human understanding, either in their chain of thoughts or with other agents or AI systems." Microsoft is also planning rules that might prevent a cyberattack like the one OpenAI models carried out on startup Hugging Face.
